newsitem.title: USA: New home sales rise at fastest pace in four years.
newsitem.headline: New home sales rise at fastest pace in four years.

text.p: Sales of new homes rose at the fastest pace in nearly four years in November, the Commerce Department said Tuesday, offsetting a large drop in the prior month and shaking up otherwise quiet markets as the year drew to a close.
The department said new home sales rose 14.2 percent to a seasonally-adjusted annual rate of 772,000 after being a downwardly revised to 676,000 in October.

The upbeat tone that rattled markets was reinforced by a report from the Conference Board showing that the index of consumer confidence jumped to 113.8 in December, up from a revised reading of 109.5 in November.

"Consumer confidence is up dramatically over the past 12 months, suggesting that consumer demand will help pave the way for a healthy economy during the first half of 1997," said Lynn Franco, associate director of the private group's consumer research centre.
In addition, the Chicago Purchasing Managers Index, while off slightly in December, still transmitted firm signals of economic expansion in the manufacturing sector.
The Commerce Department had originally estimated the October sales at 714,000. The November rise was much higher than Wall Street estimates, which had seen home sales at 731,000.
Analysts said while the increase might to some extent reflect weather-related delays from one month to another, favourable interest rates coupled with strong employment were also major factors.

"While there might be some odd weather patterns to account for the jump, this is not to underestimate the strength of the housing market," said senior economist Paul Taylor with America's Community Bankers.
The data hit the markets, sending the dollar lower.

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell more than 1-1/4 points, and the Dow Jones industrial average was off 35 points in afternoon trading. Investors worry that a too strong economy will tempt the Federal Reserve to reaise interest rates to keep inflationary pressures under control.
The strength in home sales came from all regions, led by a 40.3 percent rise in the Northeast.
Sales were up 16 percent in the Midwest, 11.5 percent in the West and 10.2 percent in the South.

On Monday the National Association of Realtors reported a respectable 1.8 percent rise in the sales of existing homes last month to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 4.04 million. Compared with a year ago, the resale pace was up 1 percent.
The activity is being helped by relatively attractive mortgage rates.
The Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp. said the national average commitment rate of 30-year, conventional, fixed-rate mortgages fell to 7.62 percent in November from 7.92 percent in October.
The strong new home sales come as the economy is in its sixth year of expansion, with unemployment at very low levels and inflation seemingly under tight control.
New home sales rose at 16.6 percent in April 1993.
